bank.answer: Next.js renders pages on the server (SSR) or at build time (SSG), so the first paint is faster and pages are SEO friendly. I would use getStaticProps for mostly static pages and SSR for user-specific data.
Use semantic HTML first, label every input, keep keyboard focus visible and in order, check colour contrast, and add ARIA only when native elements cannot do it. I test with axe and a screen reader.
A GitHub Actions workflow runs on every pull request: install, lint, run Jest tests and build. On merge to main it deploys. Failing tests block the merge.
I open one WebSocket connection, update React Query cache when messages arrive, and reconnect with backoff if it drops.
In the Task Board App I used React with TypeScript and Firebase for real-time sync. Drag-and-drop updates local state first, then writes to Firebase, so it feels instant for the 3 users.
The Weather Dashboard calls the OpenWeather API and shows a 7-day forecast with Chart.js. I cached responses for 10 minutes to avoid hitting the API limit.
I moved server state to React Query, which dedupes identical requests and caches them, so duplicate API calls dropped by about 40%.
When our team adopted TypeScript I had one week. I did the official handbook, converted one small component a day, and asked a senior to review. By the end of the sprint I shipped a fully typed form.

A teammate wanted Redux for everything. I suggested React Query for server data. We built a small prototype of both, compared the code, and the team chose React Query. We stayed friendly and it cut boilerplate.
Before a release I found a bug that broke checkout on Safari. I told my lead, reproduced it, fixed the CSS issue, added a test and we shipped on time.

default: I would break the problem into small steps, build it with React and TypeScript, test it with Jest and React Testing Library, and measure the result.
